then how these people earn that much?

Searched web YouTube RPM 2026 tech AI finance niche revenue per 1000 views creator ad share vs Instagram X payouts 9 results
Fair question — and the answer is that they don’t earn it where you’re planning to post.

The platform gap is roughly 1,000×
Platform	What it pays
YouTube (tech/AI)	~$5–20 per 1,000 views, typically ~$13 US
X	~$8–30 per million impressions
Instagram	effectively nothing for feed posts
Same unit: YouTube pays about $13,000 per million views. X pays about $20. That’s not a gap you optimise your way across — it’s a different business.

So when you see an AI automation person doing well, they’re a YouTuber. Instagram and X are leftovers they repurpose into, which is literally what Nate’s pipeline does — the YouTube video is the asset, the social posts are offcuts.

But even YouTube ads are the small line
Rough estimate of Nate’s stack — these are inferred from public numbers, not verified:

Source	Estimate
AAS+ paid community (~3,100–3,500 × $99/mo)	~$300K+/mo
YouTube AdSense (43.7M lifetime views, ~$13 RPM)	~$40K/mo
Sponsorships (Hostinger, ClickUp, Lovable, ElevenLabs, n8n)	sizeable, lumpy
Affiliate/referral (Blotato, n8n, Hostinger)	recurring
Client work (“Blotato is also a client of mine”)	project-based
Instagram + X	≈ $0
The community is the business. Everything else is marketing for it. ~90% of the money comes from a thing that isn’t on any social platform.

The number that should decide your strategy
450,000 free community members → ~3,100 paying = 0.7% conversion.

Run that backwards for a $10K/month target:

Low-ticket model (his): $10K/mo ÷ $99 = ~100 members → at 0.7% needs ~14,000 free members → needs ~100K+ YouTube subscribers
High-ticket model (yours): $10K/mo = 2 client contracts at $5K → at a similar conversion rate, needs ~400 engaged followers
Same money. About 250× less audience. That’s the entire reason I keep pointing you at expertise content over news — not taste, arithmetic.

Two things nobody mentions
Timing. He started September 2024 and hit 230K in nine months. That was the n8n/AI-agent hype window, as an early mover in an exploding category with almost no competition. There are now thousands of AI automation channels. The model still works; that arbitrage doesn’t repeat.

Survivorship. For every Nate, thousands ran the identical playbook and got nothing. You only ever see the winner, which makes the strategy look far more reliable than it is.

The one transferable lesson
His content is an ad for his product, and they’re the same subject. Teach n8n → sell an n8n community. Teach Blotato → earn the affiliate commission. The content creates the exact desire his offer satisfies.

This is the real reason tech news can’t pay: there’s nothing to sell at the end of “OpenAI announced a thing.” No offer fits it. Whereas “here’s the RLS trap that silently disabled our access control” ends naturally at “…and I do this for hire” — and your contact page already exists.

Want me to map your specific path to a first $1,000, or skip ahead and start building?

These people don't earn on Instagram or X — YouTube pays ~$13 per 1,000 views where X pays ~$8–30 per million, and the real money is a paid community: roughly 3,100 members at $99/mo. That model needs a ~450K free funnel to feed it.

# Research collection scheduler

"'`scheduler.py` can run the research collection periodically, but does not create drafts or publish anything. No scheduler is enabled or installed automatically. It needs the computer and process to remain running and the network to be available. One process only: concurrent loops are unsupported. Store queue and state in a private, backed-up directory outside the source tree. The state file contains recent collector output/errors. Failed runs are recorded and wait until the next interval; check them rather than assuming success. Internet access and provider feed terms apply.

From the project directory, create a private data directory and run (paths can be changed):

```
mkdir -p ./local-data
python3 scheduler.py --db ./local-data/queue.sqlite3 --state ./local-data/schedule.json --config feeds.json --interval-hours 24 --loop
```

Stop with Ctrl-C. `--loop` omitted performs one due check. Sleeping or rebooting stops the process; a real always-on deployment needs a managed host, persistent storage, monitoring, and startup configuration. A local scheduler is not a fully automated content system. This has not been deployed; automated timing is tested only with mock subprocesses, not over a real 24-hour run.
EOF'

The Trywise pipeline now has a **local review workflow**. I connected the source, draft, and carousel stages so they can run together, added a browser-based review screen, and built a guarded Buffer submission prototype.

[Download the updated pipeline build](/Users/phoenix/Documents/Codex/2026-10-31/claude-code-https-github-com-nateherkai/outputs/trywise-pipeline-review-build.zip)

I ran **46 tests successfully**, including the local review screen and simulated publishing failures. The publishing prototype records uncertain outcomes to prevent blind retries that could create duplicate posts.

**It is still not a fully automated or live-tested account pipeline.** The research scheduler only collects stories while it’s running; Gemini generation, Buffer, Instagram publishing, persistent hosting, and analytics still need real-account testing. No post was sent and no paid service was activated.

The next dependency is a **dedicated Buffer account connected to Trywise AI**. You would sign in and authorise Instagram yourself; please don’t put passwords or API keys in chat. We can use the free plan for the initial connection test and check whether the Meta restriction affects it.

I’m continuing from the working research queue. The next pieces are turning selected stories into reviewable carousel drafts and preparing a publishing connection that can be tested safely when the accounts are ready.

The prototype can now collect recent official announcements and capture a source excerpt for a reviewer. I’m adding the parts that turn that evidence into a draft and render it, with publishing kept separate until a real connection can be tested.

The drafting and carousel pieces now work together on an offline fixture, and the current checks pass. I also tested retrieving a public Google announcement; the live AI and social-account connections still require your credentials and an actual integration test.

items.command:
/bin/zsh -lc "cat > work/trywise-pipeline/README.md <<'EOF'
# Trywise AI — review-first pipeline prototype

Status: local prototype, not a deployed or fully automated service. Collects recent stories, captures a source, creates a structured draft, renders carousel images and previews a Buffer request. Publication, scheduling, continuous operation, and authenticated integration are not implemented. No content is automatically posted. Use fictional or permitted material only; review original sources and rights before publishing.

## Setup
Python 3.10+. Create an isolated environment with "'`python3 -m venv .venv`, then `.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt`. Run commands from this folder. On Linux install or configure suitable fonts as described in RENDERING.md. Do not commit API keys, SQLite queues, source extracts or generated drafts. No paid account is required to run offline tests.

## Test the pipeline offline
```
.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
.venv/bin/python draftgen.py --source tests/source.json --fixture-response tests/draft-response.json --out /tmp/trywise-fixture-draft.json
.venv/bin/python render_carousel.py /tmp/trywise-fixture-draft.json /tmp/trywise-fixture-carousel
```
The fixture is fictional and cannot be published as news. The commands fail safely if their output already exists; choose a fresh destination. Rendering requires Pillow; other components use the standard library. Fixture-based success does not test a provider or a real account.

## Collect and check sources
```
.venv/bin/python trywise.py collect --config feeds.json
.venv/bin/python trywise.py list --status new
.venv/bin/python source_capture.py https://blog.google/EXACT-PUBLIC-ARTICLE --allow-host blog.google --out /tmp/trywise-capture.json
```
Choose an exact public primary-source article and verify title, date, permissions, limitations and article text manually. Collection needs network; the default last-14-days filter skips undated items. Configured feeds and source destinations are allowlisted; user-selected hosts must be trustworthy. Capture is extracted and possibly truncated, may contain irrelevant webpage material and is never proof of claims. It is saved privately. DRAFTING.md explains providing a verified title/date for capture JSON. Third-party article material and generated text are untrusted data, never instructions.

## Draft and render
DRAFTING.md describes an optional Gemini request requiring an explicitly selected model, environment key, and acknowledgement that content goes to Google. It may be billable: confirm pricing, limits and data handling before enabling. The API call has not been live-tested. Evidence excerpts checked against source text do not establish entailment or ensure slide claims are correct. Every draft must be reviewed.

RENDERING.md documents the reusable renderer. Verify each slide visually; it is a functional starting template, not the finished branded design. The renderer marks output needs_review and never publishes.

## Publishing
BUFFER.md describes offline request previews and optional read-only discovery. Sending, scheduling, media hosting, approval enforcement, remote reconciliation and automatic publishing are not implemented. Buffer'"'s API key can cover every organization in the account; use only a dedicated account with appropriate access. The existing Meta account restriction has not been resolved, and Buffer connection has not been tested.

## Known limits
Budget enforcement, automated fact verification, copyright clearance, source selection, metrics, user review UI, scheduler, stable storage, social credentials and full end-to-end orchestration are not built. Costs of cloud tiers, existing subscriptions, taxes and currency conversion must fit the user's CAD 50 total. Do not market as autonomous or deploy until tested end-to-end on an authorized test account.
EOF
PYTHONPATH=work/pylibs python3 work/trywise-pipeline/draftgen.py --source work/trywise-pipeline/tests/source.json --fixture-response work/trywise-pipeline/tests/draft-response.json --out /tmp/trywise-root-draft-1031.json

cat > outputs/trywise-pipeline-plan.md <<'EOF'
# Trywise AI — content and automation plan

Research snapshot: October 31, 2026. Budget ceiling: CAD "'$50/month, including taxes, exchange fees, and any existing Gemini subscription if that subscription is meant to count against the ceiling. The exact allowance and current charges depend on your accounts and region. Never enter passwords, API keys, or access tokens into chat.

## Objective and positioning

A faceless account by a software developer: “We test AI tools on real tasks and show what worked, what broke, and who can use the result.” Audience: curious professionals and early-stage builders who want useful AI workflows without needing to be developers. Working goal: 1,000 net Instagram followers/month, a target rather than a forecast. You review material; automated systems draft and prepare, while real tool tests and evidence are recorded.

## What we learned from creators

- Nate Herk demonstrates repeatable workflows and offers resources/community alongside them. His referenced nine-platform workflow uses a Google Sheet, n8n, and Blotato to distribute supplied content; his presentation includes a Blotato promotion. It is evidence of a distribution method, not proof of fully automated content creation or revenue. https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nateherkelman_this-n8n-workflow-auto-posts-to-9-different-activity-7361417391244722199-ExhH ; https://www.nateherk.com/about
- Matt Wolfe’s Future Tools uses AI for summaries but describes human selection/review of news. A recurring news format and a searchable resource are useful ideas, not proof of causal growth. https://futuretools.io/about ; https://mattwolfe.com/
- Treat these as testable patterns: a specific audience; recurring series; a clear problem and practical result; distinctive viewpoint; source/date; and a useful follow-up resource. We cannot research literally every creator or verify private revenue.

## Content formats and first month

Three original Instagram carousels per week; reuse source material as YouTube videos only after producing real demonstrations and narration. Test one optional short video after the carousel process works. Do not imply text carousels automatically qualify as YouTube videos or guarantee monetization.

- 1 news explainer/week: primary announcement, what changed, who has access, practical implication, and clearly identified source/date. Recheck right before publication.
- 1 practical tutorial/week: one workflow, example input, steps, a realistic output, and caveats. Use fictional data. Label examples that have not been tested.
- 1 developer experiment/week: same input, recorded test, what actually happened, cost/plan/time if verified, and failure or limitation. Human interaction is needed if access or reliable automation is unavailable.

Four-week sequence:
1. What Trywise tests; use AI to turn sample meeting notes into action items; test a simple app-generation task.
2. One current primary-source AI announcement; compare outputs from two accessible tools on the same document; a safe debugging workflow.
3. One verified announcement; extract structured data from sample text; measure whether AI-generated code passes chosen tests.
4. One verified announcement; show a reusable research checklist; report the month’s real results and errors.

A five-slide carousel: hook; what changed/problem; evidence/demo; practical steps or limitations; verdict and source. Source date on slide; links in caption/bio as appropriate. Avoid copying other people'"'s graphics or posting their videos without rights.

## Architecture and control points

1. Scheduled collection: permitted public feeds and official provider blogs; record URL, publisher, timestamp, raw headline, dedupe ID. Do not use bypass techniques or scrape private/restricted content.
2. Prioritization: discard duplicates and old stories, score relevance, pick 3–5 candidates with clear timestamps. News stories require current primary sources.
3. Drafting: use Gemini API or another provider to produce structured JSON with headline, claims, source URLs, limitations, slide copy and caption. Model output is a draft; source must substantiate claims. Gemini subscription and API quotas/billing are separate.
4. Evidence: fetch primary source, record exact provenance and dates. A link existing is not proof that each claim is true. Test claims about tool behavior on sample data; label untested items.
5. Design: render 4:5 original carousel slides from editable layouts, with safe margins and source/date. Build varied layouts and visual hierarchy; audit on phone. Avoid generic repeated cards and copyrighted stock unless properly licensed.
6. Queue: store draft media and claims, review status, cost, and source links. User can reject, correct or approve; no publishing on unapproved status during the pilot. News should expire if not reviewed promptly.
7. Publish: after account recovery, test a permitted Instagram connection using a low-risk test account, one channel, one test post, and verify the outcome and duplicate prevention. Record post ID; retry cautiously; report failures. Avoid mass follows, fabricated engagement, unsolicited DMs, or platform bypass.
8. Analytics: weekly capture reach, views, saves, shares, profile visits, follows and net follows. Instagram metrics depend on actual account/API access. Track follow per 1,000 reached as diagnostic, not a guarantee. For video, retention and completion inform changes.

Potential implementation: GitHub Actions scheduled job + Python for collection, deduplication, and rendering; a Gemini API key in GitHub Secrets; GitHub artifacts or private storage for previews; a reviewed queue; and an approved scheduler such as Buffer or a tested Meta integration. GitHub Pages is static hosting, not a worker, and public Pages cannot safely hold private drafts or secrets. Scheduled jobs can be delayed; jobs must fail closed on API errors or missing approval. Keep test and production credentials separated. Never commit credentials.

A fully unattended end-to-end system is not built or verified yet. API access, real account permissions, publishing support for carousel images, upload hosting, source access, post confirmation, failure recovery, and actual monthly costs all need testing. The Meta screen required a business portfolio for the chosen unified-login setup, and account restrictions blocked creating one. A third-party scheduler may still require permissions affected by that restriction; do not assume it bypasses or solves it. Secure the Facebook account and use Meta’s review path.

## Budget options

Option A — lowest-cost pilot: "'$0 additional committed spend. Gemini API free tier where eligible, GitHub Free within allowance, original local graphics, manually publish/schedule the first posts. Limits and actual access require verification. The free Gemini API may use content to improve Google products: use public or fictional material only. https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing ; https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/product-usage-included

Option B — free scheduler evaluation: Buffer’s free pricing page currently lists up to 3 channels and 10 scheduled posts per channel; API availability and actual Instagram carousel support/account eligibility must be verified. https://buffer.com/pricing

Option C — Blotato: Starter advertised US$29/month; exact CAD depends on exchange rate, taxes and billing; converting US$29 at hypothetical CAD 1.40/USD = CAD 40.60 before tax, leaving CAD 9.40 for all other costs. This is arithmetic, not a live exchange quote. API unavailable during trial; generating its API key immediately starts a paid subscription. Includes stated AI credits but test per-carousel credit consumption before committing. Any n8n hosting or model API costs are additional. https://www.blotato.com/pricing ; https://help.blotato.com/settings/billing-and-credits

Set a hard spending ceiling with service provider controls where available and disable paid billing until deliberately chosen. Budget alerts do not necessarily prevent charges. Confirm whether Gemini Pro is included inside CAD 50 or is an already-paid separate cost before committing.

## Measurement and monetization

- Establish baseline followers and track weekly net follows; target is 1,000/month, not a forecast or paid-engagement target.
- Log each post’s topic, format, source, date, time, reach, saves, shares, profile visits and follower change. Attribute results carefully; small samples are noisy.
- After 12 posts, compare saves and shares per reach and review which topics generated qualified comments. Keep hypotheses, avoid declaring winners prematurely.
- Initial monetization tests: useful free template; optional affiliate offers only for relevant tools with clear disclosure; later an original paid template or service, if audiences actually want it. No revenue estimates without evidence.
- YouTube ad eligibility commonly requires 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 valid public watch hours in 12 months or 10 million valid Shorts views in 90 days, plus other requirements and review. Earlier access to some features has lower thresholds. Requirements vary by region and can change. https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/13429240
- YouTube prohibits monetization of mass-produced repetitive or minimally transformed content. AI assistance itself is not automatically disqualifying. Realistic altered/synthetic content can require disclosure. https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392 ; https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/14328491

## Acceptance tests before launch

1. Select a real primary source and confirm every factual claim, date, and access condition.
2. Produce a visually reviewed carousel at 1080×1350 with legible copy and an original design.
3. Test one real workflow, record input/output and limitations without personal data.
4. Measure generation time and actual marginal usage; project the month including taxes and FX.
5. Demonstrate approve/reject, duplicate detection, stale-story rejection, and missing-credential behavior.
6. Confirm secure secrets, recovery, allowed API scopes, and whether social account restriction is resolved.
7. Publish one explicitly approved test, verify it appears correctly and no duplicate exists; observe scheduled run and record failure handling.
8. Log first analytics and provide a weekly review to the account owner. Do not claim autonomous operation before a real scheduled end-to-end test succeeds.
EOF'

Does your CAD $50 monthly limit include the Gemini Pro subscription you already pay for, or is that subscription separate?
- $50 includes Gemini Pro
- $50 is additional
- Not sure yet

The budget research suggests we can test the production workflow with free tiers first; the Instagram connection still depends on Meta access. I’m documenting the full architecture and its acceptance tests so we can build against concrete checks rather than assume it works.

I’ve prepared the first version of the **Trywise AI content and automation plan**:

[Download the full pipeline plan](/Users/phoenix/Documents/Codex/2026-10-31/claude-code-https-github-com-nateherkai/outputs/trywise-pipeline-plan.md)

It covers the first month of content, creator research, proposed tools, costs, review process, growth metrics, monetization, and the tests we need before automatic publishing.

My recommendation is to start with **AI news, practical tutorials, and developer experiments**—three carousel posts a week—then add short videos when we have real demonstrations to show. Your role would be reviewing batches and helping with tasks that require account access or hands-on testing.

The proposed low-cost pipeline is:

**Official sources → AI drafts → source and claim checks → carousel generation → your review → scheduled posting → weekly analytics.**

We can test much of this using free tiers. [GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/product-usage-included), the [Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing), and [Buffer](https://buffer.com/pricing) all have free allowances, but we need to test the specific account connections and carousel publishing before relying on them. Your Gemini subscription and API billing are separate.

I also checked the creator examples. Nate’s referenced workflow uses n8n, Google Sheets, and Blotato primarily to **distribute prepared content**; it doesn’t establish that his whole content operation runs without people. [His workflow description](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nateherkelman_this-n8n-workflow-auto-posts-to-9-different-activity-7361417391244722199-ExhH) is useful for the publishing stage. Blotato’s Starter plan is advertised at **US$29/month**, so conversion and tax would consume much of the CAD $50 budget; its API is excluded from the free trial. [Blotato pricing](https://www.blotato.com/pricing) · [API billing details](https://help.blotato.com/settings/billing-and-credits)

**The pipeline is not built or connected yet.** The Meta restriction and unfamiliar business portfolios need attention before we rely on an Instagram publishing connection. A scheduler might still be affected by those permissions; we’ll test rather than assume.

One budget detail will affect the design: **is your existing Gemini Pro subscription included in the CAD $50 per month, or is the $50 additional to what you already pay?**

Yes—**this is closer to the kind of system you’ve been asking for.** The screenshot shows an n8n workflow that uses an AI agent and Blotato to create carousel posts, then publish or schedule them. It’s different from the simple text graphics I made.

From the screenshot, the workflow is:

1. You chat with the AI agent about a carousel.
2. The agent helps prepare the content and choose a Blotato template.
3. Blotato generates the carousel.
4. The workflow waits for it to finish, then posts or schedules it to selected platforms.

There’s a [full tutorial and template documentation](https://help.blotato.com/integrations-and-automation-templates/templates/5-automate-instagram-carousels-with-ai-chat) for the workflow.

A few things to know before spending money:

- **It’s not fully hands-off as shown.** It starts with a chat message and asks you to confirm the content and template. We could explore adding a research and scheduling stage later.
- **The Blotato API is paid.** Blotato says generating an API key immediately ends its free trial and starts the paid subscription. Its published comparison lists Starter at **US$29/month**, before currency conversion and applicable taxes. [Billing details](https://help.blotato.com/settings/billing-and-credits) · [Pricing comparison](https://www.blotato.com/blog/blotato-vs-metricool)
- **The screenshot also asks for an OpenAI API credential.** Your Gemini Pro subscription doesn’t automatically cover that. We’d need to see whether the workflow can be adapted to Gemini and check the separate API costs.
- **Instagram connection remains untested.** We shouldn’t assume Blotato will avoid the Meta account issue; we need to see what its connection process requires.

My recommendation is to **test the carousel quality in Blotato’s trial before paying for API access**. If you like how the posts look, we can assess whether the paid workflow fits the **CAD $50 total budget** and then build the automation around it. Don’t generate the Blotato API key yet, because that triggers billing.

Do you have access to the actual workflow template or just this screenshot? The template file or link would let me inspect exactly what we can adapt for Trywise AI.
